claims.text: HEA toughness is retained when a single-phase solid-solution microstructure is maintained.
Thermally induced elemental partitioning can form brittle intermetallic precipitates.
Formation of brittle intermetallic precipitates causes loss of toughness in HEAs.
Heat treatment that prevents precipitation can preserve toughness, whereas heat treatment that causes phase decomposition can induce embrittlement.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized, roughly equiatomic, single-phase HEA with minimal pre-existing secondary phases.
Controlled thermal aging temperature and duration are the experimental variables used to induce or avoid phase decomposition.
At approximately 600°C, the unspecified HEA remains stable.
At approximately 800°C, precipitation is expected in the unspecified HEA.
Aging exposures from 1–2 hours to more than 10 hours under constant service-representative stress can reveal the proposed behavior.
TEM and X-ray diffraction can be used to characterize precipitate size, volume fraction, and phase identity.
Elevated thermal exposure drives elemental partitioning followed by nucleation and growth of brittle intermetallic phases.
The intermetallic precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
The intermetallic precipitates act as crack-initiation sites.
Dislocation obstruction and crack initiation by precipitates reduce toughness relative to the homogenized state.
Higher-temperature or longer-duration aging will decrease fracture toughness or impact energy relative to untreated or low-temperature-aged material.
The toughness decrease will correlate with increasing precipitate volume fraction and precipitate size.
As-cast or non-aged single-phase HEAs generally exhibit high toughness because of homogeneous microstructures and enhanced dislocation mobility.
The proposed mechanism applies to HEA compositions lying within a single-phase equilibrium-stability region and may not govern when oxidation or other degradation mechanisms dominate.
The temperature-time threshold for precipitation and toughness loss is composition-dependent.
Failure to observe either brittle precipitate formation or a significant toughness decrease under conditions predicted to induce precipitation would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions predict precipitation at about 800°C, while the boundary says the hypothesis applies to compositions within a single-phase stability region under equilibrium conditions. If the composition is equilibrium-stable as a single phase at the aging temperature, the predicted thermally induced equilibrium precipitation is internally inconsistent unless the stability region is explicitly temperature-dependent or the precipitation is metastable.

The conditions present 600°C as stable and 800°C as precipitation-inducing despite no alloy composition being specified, while the uncertainty field acknowledges that these thresholds are composition-dependent and require calibration.
